# Who this is for

This book is for somebody with no lab, no relevant degree, no budget and
nobody to ask. You don't need anyone's permission to start, which is
fortunate, because there's nobody standing there to give it. If that's roughly
your situation, keep going.

If it isn't, save yourself the time. Some readers have a supervisor, a cluster
login and somebody two doors down who does this for a living. The Data
Carpentry genomics lessons will get you further than this book will: free
material, taught on the command line, on a machine somebody else set up for
you. That last part is the thing you have and this book's reader doesn't.

## What you need

Three things, and that's the whole list.

A browser, on any machine that runs a current one. Your connection is allowed
to drop, and Chapter 4 covers what to do when it does. A phone will show you
every website in Part 1, and it'll fight you the moment you have to type code.

A Google account. It's free, and it's for Colab, the notebook service this
book runs its code in. Chapter 4 is where you set that up. Nothing in Part 1
needs it: NCBI, UniProt and the rest hand their records to anyone who asks,
with no login and no email address.

About three hours a week. Each exercise prints its own time estimate before you
start it. Each chapter opens by naming the files you should already have, so a
two-week gap costs you the time it takes to find them again. You'll have a
two-week gap.

### If your only machine is a school Chromebook

Read this before the setup chapter. Google's own Colab FAQ says access for
Workspace accounts "is controlled by the Workspace on/off control accessible to
your organization's administrator". The same page says a school has to obtain
parental consent before a student under 18 uses it. So Colab may not be there
when you go looking, and the switch is on somebody else's desk.

That's a policy about who owns the account. It says nothing about your machine
and nothing about you. Part 1 needs no account at all, so you can work through
it on the school Chromebook while you sort out where your code will run.
Chapter 4 covers the school-account case and what to do instead.

### If you're paying for data by the gigabyte

Every download in this book states its size in the sentence that asks you to
start it, so you can decide before you spend anything. The dataset the whole
final project runs on is 513,592 bytes, which is about half a megabyte. A
download written into a notebook lands on Google's machine rather than yours,
so those sizes are a ceiling on what you pay rather than a bill.

## What you don't need

A math background. The arithmetic you'll do by hand is subtraction and
division. Where a real statistical method turns up, Chapter 25 uses it, names
what it assumes, and points at where the derivation lives.

Prior programming. Chapter 11 starts at what a variable is, and every example
in it is DNA, because there's no reason to learn strings twice.

An institutional login. Every database you'll pull data from is open to anybody
with a browser: NCBI, UniProt, the PDB, AlphaFold DB. None of them asks who you
work for. Chapter 23 names the one kind of archive that does, and says why you
can finish without it.

## Do you need a master's for this?

Ask on a forum whether you can do this without a degree and somebody will tell
you to get a master's. One reply on r/bioinformatics reads "Do you have no
degree or a completely unrelated degree? Very unrealistic." That answer is half
right, and the half matters.

Some jobs really do require the degree. It's printed in the posting, and no
workbook argues its way past that.

The analysis doesn't require it. NCBI serves the same record to a professor and
to a stranger, and BLAST returns the same hits either way. Nothing you're about
to do checks your credentials, because there's nothing there to check them
with.

Here's what this book can hand you. By the end you can read the methods section
of a paper in your own field and say what happened in it. You'll have a
published figure reproduced from public data, with your code somewhere a
stranger can open it. And you'll have a small analysis that nobody assigned
you.

What this book cannot hand you is a job offer ahead of a candidate with a PhD.
Anybody who sells you a job at the price of a workbook is lying to you.

One more thing, and then the subject is closed for the rest of the book. Teresa
Attwood and colleagues, writing in *Briefings in Bioinformatics* in 2019,
summarize two surveys of working practitioners. In the one run in 2013, with
about 200 respondents, 76 percent considered their bioinformatics skills to be
self-taught. Roughly 64 percent said the same in the 2014 survey, which had
about twice as many people in it.

Most of this field taught itself, so teaching yourself isn't what makes your
position unusual. The unusual part is that you're unaffiliated: no
institutional login, nobody down the hall. Every exercise ends with a check you
can run on your own answer, because that's the job a colleague would otherwise
be doing for you.

## What this book leaves out

Four subjects are missing on purpose.

Statistics stops where the arithmetic stops. You'll get counts, rates,
thresholds and one page on what running 27,179 tests at once does to a p-value.
You won't get the derivation behind the model that produced it.

Algorithm theory is out. You'll align two sequences and read what came back.
You won't write the alignment algorithm yourself, and nothing here asks you to
prove anything about it.

Wet-lab methods are out. You need no bench, no freezer and no pipette.
Somebody else generated every dataset you touch and deposited it in public,
which is the whole reason this book is possible.

The command line is out, and that one costs you something real. Plenty of
bioinformatics software is driven from a terminal. One day the tool you want
will have no web version, and you'll have to go and learn it then.

What you get in exchange is that nothing gets installed on your machine.
Exactly one line in this book installs anything, in Chapter 17, and it runs on
Google's computer. Setup is where books like this one lose people, in the first
hour, before any biology has happened. Software Carpentry's own write-up on
teaching this material gives that section the title "Is it supposed to hurt
this much?"

::: {.checkpoint}
- Decide, in one word, whether the first paragraph of this chapter describes
  you
- Name the three things this book needs from you, and check that you have each
  one
- Write down which hours of your week you're giving this, and where they are
- Say what this book can hand you at the end, and name one thing it can't
:::
